discussion.text: Papuan languages have some of the largest evidentiality systems in the world. Most are obligatory and marked on the verb, especially in Trans-New Guinea highlands languages.
2-term systems: direct vs. indirect (reported).
3-term systems: visual vs. inferential vs. reportative, as in Enga (direct/visual vs. inferred vs. reported) and Tauya.
Larger (5+ term) systems, as in Fasu and Foi: visual; non-visual sensory; reported; heard from a known source; direct participation; inferred/assumed (2–3 subtypes).
In the Text Chart, choose Mark Evidentials, then a category, then a value. Only the values can be chosen (not the categories), and the chart cell shows the value's abbreviation.

desc.en: The speaker perceived the event directly, with the senses.
The speaker saw the event.

discussion.text: Also called: eyewitness; direct.
Example: “I saw it happen.”

desc.en: The speaker heard, smelled or felt the event but did not see it.

discussion.text: Also called: non-visual; non-eyewitness.
Example: “I heard / smelled / felt it happen.”
Fasu has visual (seen) and non-visual sensory (heard) as two different suffixes.
Some systems split this value; for those languages use Auditory (AUD) and Other sensory (OSENS) instead.

desc.en: The speaker heard the event.

discussion.text: For systems that split non-visual sensory (NVSENS) into auditory and other senses.

desc.en: The speaker perceived the event by smell, touch or taste.

discussion.text: For systems that split non-visual sensory (NVSENS) into auditory and other senses.

desc.en: The speaker infers the event instead of perceiving it.

discussion.text: The most subdivided category in Papuan systems. Terms follow Aikhenvald, and San Roque & Loughnane.
Fasu has three inferential values: deduced from evidence, statement about a thought, and obvious to the speaker.

desc.en: The speaker sees the result and infers the cause.

discussion.text: Also called: inferred from evidence.
Example: “He must have gone” (I see his footprints).

desc.en: Inference from general knowledge or logic.

discussion.text: Also called: deduced; assumed; obvious.

desc.en: A gut feeling: internal reasoning that it must be so.

discussion.text: Also called: internal support.

desc.en: The speaker learned of the event from someone else.
Reported from an unspecified source.

discussion.text: Also called: reported; secondhand; hearsay (HEARSAY).
Example: “They say… / I was told…”

desc.en: A direct quotation of a named speaker. Abbreviated EV.QUOT so it isn't confused with a quote-margin marker (QUOT). Whether a quote margin is an evidential or a speech verb is an analysis decision: if you analyse quote margins as evidential marking in your language, you may want to change this abbreviation to QUOT and remove the separate quote-margin marker.

discussion.text: Example: “X said: …”

desc.en: The speaker knows who told them, as opposed to anonymous hearsay.

discussion.text: Fasu marks this as a separate value.

desc.en: The speaker knows because they did it or were involved.

discussion.text: Characteristically Papuan.

desc.en: Knowledge from the speaker's own participation in the event.

discussion.text: Also called: performative (PERF); personal-factual; ego; egophoric. These terms are used in descriptions of Foe, Oksapmin and Enga; Foe and Oksapmin are described as having a (personal-)factual value.
Example (Central Pomo style): “I caught it — I know because I did it myself.”
Avoid PERF as this marker's abbreviation: it is the usual gloss for perfect/perfective.

The known information in a sentence, the main thing being talked about or the starting point. Often (but not always) the same as the subject or the agent.
The part of the sentence that is new information in a normal, unmarked, not special sentence. This is also called "predicate focus", usually the predicate (verb plus non-topical arguments).

Narrow or broad focus, special focus. Emphasizing, asserting, or highlighting what is new or noteworthy in this sentence (the content question word and the part of the answer that replaces the content question word are in focus). The part of the assertion that is new and not presupposed.
